content.newText: ## Introduction The unit step function is a simple way to model a switch in continuous time. In its basic form, the switch turns on at $t=0$. Before the switching time, the signal is off: $$ u(t)=0\quad (t<0) $$ After the switching time, the signal is on: $$ u(t)=1\quad (t>0) $$ For example, $u(-1)=0$ because $-1$ is before the switch, while $u(2)=1$ because $2$ is after the switch. At the exact switching time, different sources use different conventions. In this course, we will use $$ u(0)=1 $$ With that convention, the basic unit step can be summarized as $$ u(t)= \begin{cases} 0, & t<0,\\ 1, & t\ge 0. \end{cases} $$ This function is a core building block for signals that start, stop, or change at specific times. Later, we will shift unit steps to create delayed switches and combine them to build rectangular pulses and other on-off signal forms. ---
content.oldText: ## Introduction to Definition of the Unit Step Function Introduce the unit step as the continuous-time switch function. In this lesson, we use it to indicate which time side of the axis is active and which side is off. Teach the rule for times before the switch: for $t<0$, the switch is off, so $u(t)=0$. Teach the rule for times after the switch: for $t>0$, the switch is on, so $u(t)=1$. Use one base case to show both sides: if $t=-1$, then $u(-1)=0$, and if $t=2$, then $u(2)=1$. Set the course convention at the boundary by declaring $u(0)=1$ for this topic line and using that same convention everywhere in this module. $$ u(t)=0\ (t<0),\ u(t)=1\ (t>0) $$ This definition is the core building block for shifted and delayed step functions, and later it will be used to construct rectangular pulses and other on-off signal forms. $$ u(0)=1\ \text{(convention for this lesson)} $$ ---

codex --help

content.text:
Skills are not invoked through a `/command` in the normal Codex CLI flow.

They’re invoked by trigger matching:

- Explicit: you name it, e.g. “use the `skill-creator` skill” or “use `$skill-creator`”.
- Implicit: your request matches a skill’s description, e.g. “install a Codex skill” triggers `skill-installer`, “make a new skill” triggers `skill-creator`, “fix GitHub PR comments” triggers the GitHub review skill.
- Plugin skills work the same way, just namespaced, like `github:gh-fix-ci`.

When a skill is invoked, Codex reads that skill’s `SKILL.md`, then loads only the referenced scripts/references/assets it needs. It’s basically a context/instruction pack, not a separate executable command.

I checked `codex --help`; there isn’t a top-level `/skill` style command shown. Skills are discovered from places like `$CODEX_HOME/skills`, usually `~/.codex/skills`, plus enabled plugin skill bundles.
